Despite there being millions upon millions of Roosevelt Dimes collected and preserved, only a portion of those coins have been preserved in excellent condition; and it is these few that collectors are after. The price you are going to be asked to pay for a specific Roosevelt Dime is completely dependent upon who is selling it and what the coin looks like. Generally speaking though, these coins are affordable for most any type of collector simply because so many still exist. On the open market today, you can expect to find Roosevelt Dimes ranging in price from as little as $1 to as much as $4 in absolutely pristine condition. Some other editions of the coin sell for even higher prices in excellent condition, but most often you will come across the $1-$4 price range. This may not seem overly expensive, but proportionate to the ten-cent face value of the coin, a $3 asking price is quite a jump. When it comes to Roosevelt Dimes, an almost universal truth is that any collector will want to purchase the coin in excellent condition. If we are speaking in terms of official coin grading, it is the Uncirculated pieces that are most desired by collectors. The pieces that were almost immediately put under lock and key after minting are so desired because of their appearance. Taking on the look of a coin that was minted recently, these pieces are truly a wonder to behold. When holding and viewing these coins, you will notice that all of the coin’s raised imagery and inscriptions are perfectly intact. If this coin was extremely aged and had been heavily circulated, the surfaces of the coin would be void of texture and generally smooth to the touch. By closely analyzing the surfaces of a given coin, you are able to determine a rough grade. If the coin in question is shiny and fully of texture, the chances that it is an Uncirculated piece are somewhat high. The only way to officially know the grade of a coin is to have it judged by a professional company, but a keen eye will be able to pick out imperfections and other things that may detract from the overall value. Though it is impossible to predict the value of Roosevelt Dimes many years down the road, history has shown us that coins like this only become more expensive to acquire as time moves on. In the case of the Roosevelt Dime, the fact that the coin has not been produced since the 1960s means that, with each passing year, there are only going to be fewer and fewer coins on the market. For this reason, there has never been a better time than now for you to get your hands on a well-preserved Roosevelt Dime. If you find yourself sitting here ten years from now looking to make a purchase, do not be surprised if the price of the coin has gone up dramatically. In addition to there simply not being that many Roosevelt Dimes left on the market with each year that passes, there will be even fewer well-preserved coins, so now is really the time to act. Initially struck in 90% silver until 1964 before transitioning to copper-nickel, Roosevelt dimes offer collectors diverse collecting opportunities spanning over 75 years of production. From key dates like the 1949-S and elusive varieties like the 1964 Special Mint Set dime to modern treasures such as the 1996-W, these coins capture the legacy of Roosevelt's leadership while providing accessible yet rewarding collecting challenges for both novice and advanced numismatists seeking to build comprehensive dime collections. Origin & History The Roosevelt dime arose from the nation's desire to honor President Franklin D. Roosevelt after his death in April 1945. As the leader who guided America through both the Great Depression and most of World War II, Roosevelt had a personal connection to the dime denomination through his founding of the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis (later renamed the March of Dimes), which raised funds for polio research and treatment—a disease Roosevelt himself battled. Less than a month after Roosevelt's death, Representative James Hobson Morrison introduced legislation to replace the Mercury dime with a design honoring the late president. The bill quickly gained support and was signed into law by President Harry S. Truman. Chief Engraver John R. Sinnock was tasked with creating the design, though controversy would later emerge regarding his inspiration sources, with some claiming he drew from sculptor Selma Burke's bronze relief portrait or photographer Marcel Sternberger's 1936 photograph of Roosevelt. Production began in 1946 with the Philadelphia, Denver, and San Francisco mints producing over 350 million dimes that first year. From 1946 through 1964, Roosevelt dimes were struck in 90% silver and 10% copper. The Coinage Act of 1965, responding to rising silver prices, changed the composition to copper-nickel clad (75% copper, 25% nickel over a pure copper core), which continues in circulation coins today. Since 1992, the U.S. Mint has also produced special silver proof versions for collectors, initially in 90% silver and, since 2019, in 99.9% fine silver. Design Elements The obverse of the Roosevelt dime features a left-facing profile portrait of Franklin D. Roosevelt, conveying dignity and strength through its clean, classical design. "LIBERTY" appears along the upper rim in front of Roosevelt's face, while "IN GOD WE TRUST" is positioned in smaller letters below the chin. The date is located at the lower right, with designer John R. Sinnock's initials "JS" subtly placed just below the neckline truncation. These initials sparked controversy when the coin was first released, with some erroneously suggesting they represented Joseph Stalin during the early Cold War tensions. The reverse design elements have remained consistent throughout the series: - 1946-Present: The reverse features a torch with flowing flame at center, symbolizing liberty, flanked by an olive branch (representing peace) on the left and an oak branch (representing strength and independence) on the right—creating a design unique among circulating U.S. coinage. The legend "UNITED STATES OF AMERICA" arcs around the top rim, while "ONE DIME" appears at the bottom, separated by centered dots. - Mint Marks: On silver issues (1946-1964), the mint mark appears on the reverse, positioned to the right of the torch's base. After 1964, mint marks were moved to the obverse, appearing below the date. - Composition Changes: While not visibly different, the composition shifted from 90% silver (1946-1964) to copper-nickel clad (1965-present), slightly altering the coin's color from silver-white to silver-gray.
